Dr Gibbs, we have heard from previous witnesses about the monitors that were in place in the neonatal unit back in June 2015 and the type of readings that they would display and the, I think, a two-tier alarm system that they contain.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Firstly, can I ask, are you aware whether those monitors would record, firstly, the readings that would have been displayed in real time in relation to the relevant baby?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: As far as I can recall, yes, in real time.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Would it be possible to go back into the monitor and produce an audit or a record of previous readings over perhaps the preceding time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm not sure.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If you're not sure, please don't --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If you're not sure -- if you happened to know the answer --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm not sure.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I think what is really wanted -- obviously when an alarm goes off, the display will still be there on the screen?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: One can then look at the screen and see why the alarm's gone off.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But what we really need to know is: is a recording made of the readings, an ongoing reading?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: A bit like CCTV records for a period of 30 days or something like that, then it wipes out and starts again.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Do you know whether at that time those machines recorded or not?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I don't think they did. There were different monitors that could be used and an oxygen saturation monitor, a separate one, can look back an hour or so. But if the oxygen saturation is being recorded through the main Philips monitor with all the other parameters, I don't think, but I'm not sure, that you can go back and look at a record.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I think the specific question was whether there would be a record of the alarm ever being activated on that Philips monitor. Would you be able to assist with that?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Activated and deactivated.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Whether it had been activated at some point in time?
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Would it be possible to interrogate the monitor and --
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm not aware that it is possible and I have never done so in my practice.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: As far as I'm aware, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So what there is is there will be a display on the screen of a bell symbol to indicate that an alarm's gone off, but with a line through it --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: To show that it's been cancelled.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Dr Gibbs I'm going to ask you some questions on behalf of Ms Letby.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Before we come to questions about [Baby C], I'd just like to ask you something about the arrangement for the consultants at the hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: At the time we're talking, 2015 to June 2016, there were seven consultants in paediatrics at the Countess of Chester, weren't there?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You were one of those consultants?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: They were all consultant paediatricians; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: None of them were specialist consultants in neonatology; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not specialists. All had had neonatal training suitable for a district general hospital.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Those seven consultants were shared across the children's ward, the maternity ward and the neonatal unit; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: How many children's wards are there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: One.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So it's one children's ward, one maternity ward --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- and one neonatal unit?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Each week, one of those seven consultants would be designated paediatrician of the week, wouldn't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The other six would remain ostensibly with responsibilities on the children's ward and the maternity unit; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No. The consultant of the week duties covered both the paediatric ward and the neonatal unit and, indeed, the maternity ward. We didn't have a lot of activity on the maternity ward that's obviously the mothers under the obstetricians. Most of the babies on the maternity ward are well. If they were particularly unwell they'd come down to the neonatal unit. So our activity was focused on the neonatal unit and the paediatric ward as paediatrician of the week.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I just want to be clear: one of the consultants was paediatrician of the week for the neonatal unit?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And the neonatal unit -- I'll fairly sure in 2015/2016 the paediatrician of the week covered both the paediatric ward and the neonatal unit. Arrangements have changed since then but that's what existed at the time we are considering these babies.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And what would the other six consultants be in terms of duties then? Where would they be?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: They would be running their clinics regularly. The paediatrician of the week would not have any routine planned clinics for that week. We took it in turn because the NHS never closes, it's a 24-hour, 365-day a week (sic) service, so the consultant of the week couldn't be on call for the entire week, 24 hours, 7 days in a row, so the other consultants took it in turns to cover from the evening and overnight each day so the consultant of the week covered the wards during the daytime and each of the other consultants took it in turns to be on call to cover for problems overnight.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Were the consultants based, if that's the right word, on the paediatric ward, the children's ward?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, based on both, but we did spend more time on the paediatric ward than on the neonatal unit often -- it depended what was happening on the neonatal unit -- because the number of admissions to the paediatric ward was much higher than the number of admissions each week to the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The paediatrician of the week would be available between 8.30 and 4.30 pm, something like that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. And also, having talked about the arrangement for the evening and overnight, the paediatrician of the week would also do one 24-hour cover at the weekend as well.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: In terms of ward rounds, would there be two ward rounds by the consultant or consultants on the neonatal unit each week, Wednesday and Saturday?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry?
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Wednesday and Saturday.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, Wednesday and Sunday.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Wednesday and Sunday, right. By contrast, there would be five weekly ward rounds on the paediatrics ward wouldn't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Usually, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: As a general rule, would there always be a doctor, whether it's a senior house officer, a registrar or a consultant, on the children's ward?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There would always be a registrar and a senior house officer, sometimes more than one. The consultant would be there
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: on the ward during ward rounds and will come back to the ward, if requested, for particular problems.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But the consultant wasn't based permanently on the paediatric ward.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Taking the consultant out of it, would there always be a registrar on the children's ward?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, covering the children's ward, not necessarily physically there present the whole time. A fair proportion of the time, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: There wouldn't always be a registrar on the neonatal unit, would there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There should have been. Yes, there should have been.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Was it the case that the weight of consultant presence was based around the children's ward and the maternity unit rather than the neonatal unit?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: As I've mentioned, the maternity unit didn't really feature much in our workload, so it's the neonatal unit and the paediatric ward. Our presence would depend on need. So if there are particular concerns on the neonatal unit, the consultant of the week would spend more time on the neonatal unit. But as I've mentioned, the number of admissions and the turnover was much higher on the paediatric ward than the neonatal unit, consequently the consultant of the week tended to spend more time on the paediatric ward than the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And likewise if they were on duty, the other six consultants would spend more time on the children's ward than the neonatal unit, wouldn't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Depending on what was happening. If there were particular concerns on the neonatal unit that might reverse.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But as a general rule, as a starting point, the weight of the consultants is in the paediatric unit and the children's ward isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Now, would you agree that up to the period of July 2016 consultant cover was quite stretched for the neonatal unit?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Well, after the unit had been redesignated a level 1, after July 2016, didn't you receive more consultants, as it happens, at the Countess of Chester?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, but we had applied for and requested more consultants for several years before 2015.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes, which implies therefore the cover was stretched in some way, doesn't it, before then?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Our level of cover was fairly typical for a district general hospital level 2 unit.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I'm keen to know what the cover -- what the reality of the cover was at the Countess of Chester however it's equated to the rest of the NHS. So far as the Countess of Chester was concerned, you had wanted additional consultants to cover the neonatal unit and the paediatric unit for some time, hadn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And you in fact got them, certainly you got one more, after the unit had actually been redesignated a level 1, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, but we had been applying for more long before that.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Did you get two, in fact, after it had been redesignated a level 1?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Over the next few years, yes. I'm a little hazy on exact numbers because, as we increased consultant numbers, a number of the new consultants were less than full time. So if we're talking about full time -- I think in the end we went up to nine whole time equivalents.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: One of which, in fact, was a consultant neonatologist, wasn't it? Is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No. I think -- I'm trying to think. I'm trying to remember who you're referring to. No, we were all general paediatricians who had done training in neonates appropriate for a district general hospital.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: When it came to the two additional consultants, after 2016, was application made for one of them to be a consultant neonatologist? Let me start with that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I can't remember the job descriptions for the new consultants after 2016. All of the consultants at the Countess of Chester Hospital, until I retired towards the end of 2019,
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: were general paediatricians who had also trained in neonatology. All of the paediatricians undertook general paediatric duties as well as neonatal duties. None of my colleagues did only neonates.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: In any event, is this correct, that after the time when the unit was actually redesignated level 1, the consultant cover in fact increased by two additional consultants?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, because that had been planned for many years.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The first thing is: did it increase by two? And the answer is yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And then that was something that had been requested for some years, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So at the point when the acuity of the children that you were looking after had been reduced, you then got additional consultants; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. But it wasn't because the acuity had been reduced, it had been planned for some years.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes. It would have been much better if you'd had them before then, wouldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: As for most district general hospitals that constantly struggle against understaffing across all specialties in the NHS, yes, every specialty wants more staff.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes. And therefore, if it was an improvement after that event, it's something you would have wanted before the redesignation, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We had wanted it, but partly it's because of the pressure of the European Working Time Directive, that we were all working too many hours, so we wanted to increase the number of staff, so we could reduce the number of hours we were working.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I'm not asking for the explanation behind it, Dr Gibbs, I'm going to establish this, if that's all right, that you had wanted two additional consultants for some time, hadn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, along with most other district general hospitals in the same position as us, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: [Baby C] was on the limit of what you could accept at the Countess of Chester by virtue of his weight alone, wasn't he, 800 grams?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Just looking at his weight, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes. In other words, before we even come to consider any other issues in relation to [Baby C], he was on the borderline, wasn't he?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Just with respect to his weight, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes. But the point is, there were other issues associated with [Baby C] in addition to his weight, weren't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That he was premature you mean?
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That's one issue, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, and he was well within the range of premature babies we treated at the Countess of Chester.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: He had reverse end-diastolic flow; that's correct, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's probably why he had a low weight and that was related, that's the same problem.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That raised the potential for abdominal problems, didn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It increases the chance of necrotising enterocolitis (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: It increases the chance of other abdominal problems actually, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Just because he's low weight?
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: No, his overall condition, including the reverse EDF.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, it's my understanding that poor circulation from the placenta to the baby, which was manifest in [Baby C] with reverse EDF, predisposes mainly to necrotising enterocolitis.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We'll come to other issues shortly and let me ask for your help when I get to those.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: He would have been -- it's also inevitable, isn't it, with a baby like [Baby C], that he is going to have problems with infection in hospital, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Well, he did have, didn't he?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: He had suspected infection early on.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: He had markers for infection, didn't he?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: He had mild to moderately raised markers for infection, but they can also be markers for inflammation and not always infection.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: He's a tiny little baby. Is that not considered some kind of concern if there are raised markers for infection?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: As it is in all babies.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So it is considered a concern is it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, if a patient has suspected infection, which we deal with very commonly on the neonatal unit and have done for many years.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Do you not think he would have been better placed, when you look at the whole thing in hindsight now, in a tertiary unit rather than Countess of Chester?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That depends on what caused his sudden collapse and unexpected death.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: In any event, given his health complications, don't you think he would have been better placed at a tertiary unit for the care that he was going to need?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You don't?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Whose decision was it that he should stay at the Countess of Chester?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I... It's 7 years ago, I can't remember exactly who made the decision and so on. It's a combination between the obstetrician looking after [Baby C]'s mother, the most senior nurse around at the time a baby is born, and the consultant of the week, which was me at the time.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So does that mean you would have had input into whether or not he stayed at the Countess of Chester or went to a tertiary unit?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Usually, yes, but I can't remember any discussions held about that for [Baby C] 7 years ago.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I'm not going to ask you to remember the wording of any discussions 7 years ago.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I've asked you about infection. Yesterday you were asked about aspirates, gastric aspirates. Do you remember those questions?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You indicated you were aware that there were some aspirates during the period that he was at the Countess of Chester; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We're able to get a note of the evidence as it goes along in this case. So I'm just looking at this. Your view was that there wasn't any concern because they weren't copious; is that fair?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And you explained to the jury that the stomach naturally produces acid?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, and mucus and acid, amongst other secretions.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Mucus and acid.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And that the concerns for aspirates could be met by giving him ranitidine; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Partly. That's to reduce any inflammation from the acid; it doesn't stop the actual secretions.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Ranitidine was used for conditions in connection with indigestion, heartburn, acid reflux; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If they were vomiting it, yes.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You have mentioned intestinal obstruction.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Let's think about that, please. blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Smoother, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: All right. So I just acknowledge that difference.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And the rectum to the anus and then out of the body?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So when we are hearing reference to the small intestine and the large intestine, that's just to help us with the layout there, Dr Gibbs.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: It should, if the gut is functioning correctly, continue to travel that way, all the way around the large intestine, down round to the rectum, and then out, unless it's absorbed on the way?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: So they looked at the whole of this.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm going to ask you about "marked gaseous distension of the stomach and proximal small bowel".
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can we go back to the image, please, at 1996, Mr Murphy?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We know from what the radiologist has said, from the image, that there is a significant amount of gas in the stomach and the small intestine, don't we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We can see the stomach enlarged towards the top of the picture, the oval-shaped area?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And then the small intestine, proximal small intestine, below that, the area of that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What we don't have is any air that has entered into the large intestine, the colon, do we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not obviously, no.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And we're perhaps all a bit more familiar with where the rectum will be and there's no air in the rectum area down the end of the gut, is there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There's a very small, little dark patch just where the mark up to the north-west of the -- yes, about there (indicating).
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes. But whereas we can see the position of air elsewhere we don't have it running through to the rectum, do we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There's much more air in the proximal small bowel and the stomach. There are little patches of air further down.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If air is being introduced into [Baby C], causing this to happen, ordinarily you would expect air to pass through stomach, small intestine, large intestine, wouldn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That hasn't happened here, has it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There are small amounts of air, as I mentioned before, going down into the rectum.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We don't have air passing from the stomach to the small intestine and filling the large intestine, do we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not as much in the large intestine, no.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Well, the report from the consultant radiologist says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Air in the stomach and the small proximal small intestine", doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And I asked you moments ago about air in the large intestine and you agreed it doesn't appear to show air in the large intestine?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It doesn't appear to but it's difficult to distinguish the large from the small intestine on a plain X-ray.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And we don't have air travelling down -- apart from one little dot there, we don't have air travelling down through the rectum, do we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There's not much air down there.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So whatever possible explanations there are for that, one possible explanation for what we see is that there is some sort of blockage stopping air from moving from the small intestine to the large intestine, isn't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's one possible explanation but air does get absorbed from the intestine, as it passes through, back into the body. The oxygen in the air gets absorbed into the intestinal wall.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We can see a significant marked distension of the stomach and the small intestine, can't we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, which commonly happens in babies who have been given ventilatory support. And I think at this time [Baby C] was on CPAP.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: However it's happened, do you agree what we can see is consistent with that air not moving through to the large intestine, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not as much air moving through to the large intestine, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That's consistent with an intestinal blockage, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That is a possible explanation.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And you have explained to us that the production of dark bile and vomit, one possible explanation for that is an intestinal blockage, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Repeated dark-stained vomiting, yes --
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: -- but [Baby C] didn't have that.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I'm not going to repeat the cross-examination. We've been over it, Dr Gibbs.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: He had one vomit.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What we have is consistent with the blockage in the intestines or into the large bowel, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's one explanation of what is shown on the X-ray, but I did mention previously you need to examine the patient.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes. Or even send the patient for examination with a paediatric surgeon?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If there was a -- if there was a high chance -- no, a reasonable chance the baby had a blocked intestine.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And that's entirely consistent with what we see, isn't it? Help us, Dr Gibbs: that's consistent with it, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's one possibility but it's more likely that it is air bleeding blown down into his stomach and intestine because of his CPAP.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That might be how it got there. But that doesn't make any difference to the fact it could be an intestinal blockage that prevents it from moving through does it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But when there is an intestinal blockage, which you are suggesting this X-ray shows, the abdomen is usually very distended. As so far as I recall, the registrars had examined [Baby C] probably on the 11th/12th, I examined him on the 13th, he had a soft non-distended abdomen.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If [Baby C] had been on CPAP on the 12th, which he was, and if the CPAP had been blowing air into him, which CPAP does, that could cause a distension, couldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And if the nurse dealing with it was failing to aspirate the tube or it wasn't on free drainage, that would allow the stomach to distend as the air went in, wouldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Just remind us, we've already seen from when Yvonne Griffiths was on, we don't have a record of aspirations for the period leading up to 18.00 on 12 June. That's a feature of the evidence. Right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: After 18.00, on 12 June, we have seen dark bile aspirates being measured on the clinical charts, haven't we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. But in intestinal obstruction usually those aspirates progressively increase and they didn't in [Baby C].
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Just dealing with the question of air and soft bellies, if [Baby C] is being aspirated or his NGT is on free drainage, after this X-ray, then that would account for his abdomen not distending in the same way?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm sorry to pause here. If the baby has an intestinal obstruction, then a normal nasogastric tube, which is very thin, would not relieve the obstruction.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I'm not talking about the obstruction, just the extraction of air as it goes in on the CPAP, Dr Gibbs.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It will remove air going in from the CPAP if it's excessive, won't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The nasogastric tube would help to do that, yes, but air also comes up naturally up through the oesophagus.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes. But if the cause of distension is air entering via CPAP; yes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And if [Baby C] is on free drainage or his stomach is being aspirated, that might take out the air and stop CPAP belly or distension from happening; yes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It would reduce CPAP belly. The nasogastric tube is very thin, about a millimetre or two across. The oesophagus in a little 800 gram baby like [Baby C] is probably a centimetre or so across. More air comes up the oesophagus than comes up the nasogastric tube.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I want to deal with what I was asking you, I just want to ask about that, about intestinal blockage, which is something you had referred to with dark bile as a possibility.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Dark bile vomiting, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Which we've had. What's an volvulus, please?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's when the bowel twists on itself, so almost does a corkscrew and becomes blocked.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If the bowel is properly formed, as it moves in the way that we've seen, the structure of it, it's held in place on these -- is it the mesentery?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The mesentery is a connective tissue that holds the bits of bowel we are looking at in the right place in the abdomen, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The small bowel, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The small bowel, yes. An volvulus is, did you say that's a loop or a twist in the intestine?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, the intestine twists and you get a loop of grossly distended small intestine.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Can there be an volvulus in the large intestine?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not usually because it doesn't have this mesentery. It is fixed to the back wall of the abdomen.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: All right. You're not familiar with any of the findings from the post-mortem, are you, Dr Gibbs, of Dr Kokai?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I have seen the post-mortem report, yes -- I mean, I haven't looked at [Baby C]'s notes since I did my statement 5 years ago. But before that, following [Baby C]'s death, as part of trying to review what had happened, of course I looked at the coroner's report or the post-mortem report when the coroner released it, which was, I think, a couple of months after [Baby C]'s death.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes. I'm not going to ask you to remember the contents of that, I'll deal with that another way. That comes some months afterwards.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In any event, if air has entered [Baby C] with sufficient pressure to create the distension that we can see on this
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: particular photograph, a clear explanation for the air not continuing is some sort of obstruction somewhere along the bowel, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's one possibility. That's not the explanation.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Usually, the small bowel in a volvulus is much more distended than this. There is one very distended loop of bowel which I don't see on [Baby C]'s X-ray.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I'm just asking you to help us with why it is the air doesn't move through the whole of the intestine.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: As I said, the air gets absorbed as it passes down the intestine because the oxygen gets absorbed out of the air.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That's one explanation?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But that's not all of the air, that's only the oxygen, one-fifth of the volume of air.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If there was -- I'll just ask this: if there had been an obstruction there, certainly no test or exploration undertaken at the Countess of Chester Hospital had been designed to look for it, had it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct, apart from this plain X-ray.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And if dark bile and vomit is a red flag, potentially, for obstruction, that's something that could have been done relatively early, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Once those problems had appeared, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That's a potential mistake not having done that, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, I think we've discussed repeatedly there was not repeated bile-stained vomiting. There was one vomit recorded in [Baby C]. And bile-stained aspirates, as I said several times, can happen as part of a normal response in a baby due to regurgitating bile.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I'm not going to repeat the questions that I've asked.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I have asked them and you've answered them. I'll move to the next thing.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: [Baby C] didn't actually have his bowels open at any time during his life, did he?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm not aware of that. I'm not surprised because he hadn't been fed.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Three days without any bowel opening, not even from any natural process with post-natal ejection, nothing happened, did it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's unusual but [Baby C] had not been fed so it doesn't stimulate -- you need to feed a baby to stimulate the bowel, to get it going well.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yon are saying this is a bowel that might have been able to absorb quantities of oxygen, aren't you, Dr Gibbs?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, as any bowel can.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: On the face of it, one would have expected, within 3 days, something passing out of his bowels?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Often that would be the case.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: As it happens, something not passing out of his bowels in that way may be consistent with a blockage, mightn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It might be, but as I've mentioned, [Baby C] was not being fed. So if you're not feeding a baby, you're not going to get much bowel motions.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: No, but you know that even with not feeding a baby there may be some ejection of meconium or something like that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That didn't happen, did it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I can't remember from 7 years ago, but if you say that's what the notes show, that's what the notes show, and it didn't happen.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I am welcome to be corrected if I'm wrong but we have looked through it and tried to find something other than NBO, which is no bowel opening, and that's the only thing we see -at least the only thing I've seen there.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I invite correction if I'm at all wrong about that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In terms of reviewing by consultant, can we go please to slide 77.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: This is the note by Dr Ogden, 9.30 in the morning on 13 June. If we scroll down it, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Over the page if we would, please. Just down to the bottom of the page. We can see down there, now it's the 13th, we've got a note saying that [Baby C] had been reviewed by you and he'd been given ranitidine and to:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Hold off feeds this PM if aspirate not getting worse."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think that's "review", we were told.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "Reviewed this pm" --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, sorry, my Lord. My mistake. It is "hold off feeds" and I have missed off the "RV":
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "Review this PM if aspirate not getting worse.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Start trophic feeds, if worsens..."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Is that "repeat abdominal X-ray"?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "And change antibiotics"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: He didn't go for another abdominal X-ray at this point, did he?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: On the notes this appears to be the first review by any consultant of [Baby C]. We haven't seen an entry for a consultant before this point, Dr Gibbs. All right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Is that -- I can't remember his notes from 7 years ago.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I'm quite content to go through them just to assist you, but if no issue is being taken with it, this is the first entry we see referencing you after admission.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I accept that then. But as I did say, it was my usual practice to go to the neonatal unit after every ward round on the paediatric ward to discuss with the nurses and the junior doctors there if any of the babies are causing concern. I would be very surprised if I hadn't looked at [Baby C] but I obviously hadn't examined him comprehensively because I have written nothing in the notes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: There should be some sort of note indicating a review by a consultant if there has been a thorough review, shouldn't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, if I'd examined him.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And when it's a review, like the review we have here, at this point would you look at the available information relating to [Baby C] at his cot side?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. I wouldn't necessarily review every investigation that had been done since he was born but I would look at him at that time, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And it sometimes happens, doesn't it, that the consultant may rely on the registrar or other doctor present to write down the findings of the review; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Does that mean that what Sally Ogden has written before the reference to you may be material that relates to your review of [Baby C] or can you not say?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I can't say but it would usually -- if I had disagreed with any of her findings or added to the findings, she should have made a note of that.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Isn't it the case that if it is almost 3 days in that [Baby C] was first reviewed by a consultant, isn't that a little too long to wait for a baby who's in [Baby C]'s condition?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: As I said, it was my normal practice to -- well, every baby has been reviewed morning and evening at the handover and that would have included [Baby C] since he was born on the Wednesday, whenever it was, the 10th.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And it's my normal practice to go to the neonatal unit after the paediatric ward rounds, so he would have been reviewed by me.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Sometimes before this point you're saying?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, but not examined by me.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If he was reviewed -- to what extent would you have reviewed him if it was before this point where we can actually see an entry?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I would check with the nurse looking after him, and the junior doctors, that they were happy with his progress.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So not a review in terms of you examining him yourself and going through the available information?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's right. If that had happened then it should have been recorded.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes, all right. That's why I asked: would it not be preferable for a baby like [Baby C] to have the benefit of a review by a senior consultant like you at a time before this?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think you have to be careful with the use of words. Review. He said he was reviewing but he didn't examine.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I apologise.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: If that's the question, would have been examined --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It is.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: -- then put that question.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I will.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Wouldn't it be preferable for [Baby C] to have an examination by a consultant like you at a point before this, Dr Gibbs?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It would have been preferable if there'd been significant concerns about him and if he'd not been examined by any of the registrars.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Well, I'm going to suggest to you there should have been a closer level of examination by a more specialist doctor than took place before this point for [Baby C].
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If we had, as we -- if we had consultants to do the neonatal ward round every day as well as doing the paediatric ward round every day that would have happened, but our practice at that time at the Countess of Chester Hospital was similar to many other level 2 neonatal units in a district general hospital.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I'm going to ask to go to slide 213, please. That's page 1924.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I just want to ask you a little bit about what happened during the resuscitation process, Dr Gibbs. If we go down to Dr Davis' note which is in the lower part of this page, the records we have indicate that the collapse, [Baby C]'s collapse, took place at 23.15.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's in the note by Nurse Ellis. If we look here, we can see that Dr Davis has arrived at about 23.27.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: She says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "23.26. Crash bleeped."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Then she arrived a minute later, so about 11 minutes after the collapse took place.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If we just carry on going down Dr Davis' note, please, to:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Heart rate 79 on monitor. Chest compressions stopped. No HR/RR on auscultation."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is there any indication there as to whether or not or for how long [Baby C] may have been without oxygen up to that point? Is that something that can be obtained from those notes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: From this?
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Whether he'd been administered oxygen?
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Was he receiving oxygen over the period when we're waiting for Dr Davis to get there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: He ought to have been, yes, but if Dr Davis wasn't there, she can't record that.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Does it indicate whether he is receiving it at the time she got there? Let me ask you that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It doesn't state that in Dr Davis' retrospective notes here. But it would be very surprising if he wasn't receiving oxygen.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You managed to intubate [Baby C] at the first attempt, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Apparently so. I can't remember the details, no.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: No one is disputing that. You were asked yesterday a little bit about the process and the purpose of intubating a baby. What you said was:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "It's more effective by ETT, endotracheal tube, than Neopuff."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. But I also said Neopuff is still effective.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes, it can be good, can't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But as it happens, intubation with an endotracheal tube can be more effective?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, particularly in a prolonged resuscitation, because of the problem of blowing oxygen and air down into the stomach and distending the stomach, which squashes the chest a little.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right. This is quite a prolonged resuscitation, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. But initially, that problem of compressing the lungs from Neopuff ventilation isn't a problem at the beginning of the resuscitation. The longer it continues, the better it is, if possible, to have endotracheal intubation, which is what happened for [Baby C].
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes. That happened once you had arrived and you were able to do that; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Which was -- if we go to the time you arrived, please, scroll up the page, please.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, about 00.35 -- no, 23.35.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: 23.35. So you arrived about 20 minutes after the collapse?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: All right. So there may have been some period with the Neopuff blowing air possibly into the stomach before he was intubated?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, as well as blowing air and oxygen down into the lungs. Even if I hadn't been able to intubate [Baby C], Neopuff ventilation could have continued.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I want to ask you some questions about the debrief notes that you were taken to yesterday. They start at slide 308, page 1927.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: A general point about this process that we see recorded here. This is a debrief involving those people who were involved in the resuscitation and also Eirian Powell. Was she the ward manager?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. But not necessarily all of the people because -trying to get -- they are trying to coordinate everybody together on different shifts.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: This operates very much as a review by those who were involved looking through the available information to see if there's any understanding of what took place?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: This is reviewing the actual collapse and resuscitation, not the whole of [Baby C]'s short life.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That was done later.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But it does pick out certain features that are considered possibly relevant because we can see looking down there, things like CRP, which is the inflammatory marker. That's recorded, suggesting infection, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And that's something that pre-exists before the actual collapse?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. This wasn't a comprehensive review, but we were looking for explanations for [Baby C]'s collapse, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: It's not an independent assessment where somebody else has come in to work out or look at all the available information of what happened, is it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No. It's a debrief of the actual traumatic event of [Baby C]'s collapse and failed resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And it's created by a number of those, largely, who were involved in that process?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is this debrief always included as part of the clinical notes when a debrief does take place?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It should be. When I say it should be, by the time we got people together for this debrief it's just over 2 weeks after [Baby C]'s death and sometimes the notes have disappeared around the hospital, off to the pathologist for the post-mortem, or elsewhere and so sometimes notes aren't available. "I have also mentioned that [Baby C]'s abdomen appeared distended, which is something else that we look at with new babies, but it was soft to firm, so although it is not firm, it is soft to firm. One of the things that we always look out for in premature babies is something called NEC, necrotising enterocolitis, which is when the gut becomes necrotic for one reason or another. We always check whether the tummy is soft and whether it is distended.

It can look loopy in the tummy, but I have not documented that. If I had seen anything like that I would have documented it, but I have only documented 'soft to firm'.

blocks.text: Well, he was a vulnerable baby because he was preterm, 30 weeks' gestation, and on top of that he had IUGR, in other words his growth was retarded, so he was 800 grams at birth, whereas the average weight for a 30-weeker is about 1,400 grams. So therefore he had two significant risk factors in relation to his status at the time of his birth. This would mean admission to a neonatal unit and that he would need careful management, both with regard to nursing care, medical care and the monitoring that goes with all of that, over a period of many weeks.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And during that time there would be -- he was at risk for a number of complications that we associated with prematurity.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. Can you give us in a list the relevant risks, so not every conceivable risk, Dr Evans, but so far as his presentation was concerned?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right. The commonest risk is to do with breathing, with his respiratory system, and lots of premature babies require support with breathing. So therefore there was a breathing problem.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The second big risk related to feeding because the gastrointestinal tract is not necessarily geared to accept milk. Therefore there are feeding difficulties, which is why babies require intravenous nutrition.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The third concern related to infection and the infection could be respiratory, in other words a lung infection, or it could be an infection somewhere else.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The fourth complication would be -- sorry, and then in relation to the feeding difficulties, given his growth retardation he was particularly at risk from this condition we've heard a lot about called NEC, necrotising enterocolitis.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The fourth concern would be metabolic and, in particular, concerns that his glucose values would stay within normal and also he was at risk of jaundice, in other words his bilirubin value was likely to cause concerns. So those were the main concerns as he would have arrived on the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: All right. I'd like to deal with those four headings of concern one by one, if we may, and look at [Baby C]'s progress from birth to collapse.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So dealing first with the issue of breathing, we've heard all the records and the witnesses' accounts of [Baby C]'s presentation so far as breathing was concerned over the period of his whole life.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. His breathing situation stabilised over a number of days and, by that, I mean two main things. blocks.text: So therefore that was a very, very encouraging sign that he was able to cope, breathing more or less on his own, and the other good sign was that the percentage of oxygen that he required continued to decrease. blocks.text: Yes. First of all, all babies who are 10 weeks premature require nasogastric feeding. Their sucking reflex and their swallowing reflex is insufficiently developed, therefore they need what we call enteral feeding, milk from the -- through the nasogastric tube into the stomach.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: If they cannot tolerate that or there's a risk to giving oral feeds too early, then it is clinical practice to give what we call TPN, total parenteral feeding, basically giving all the nutrition intravenously. Given that [Baby C] was at risk of NEC, necrotising enterocolitis, the clinical team chose to feed him intravenously, which was the right thing to do.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So you then need to monitor the baby very carefully to make sure that he does not develop any gastrointestinal problems, particularly NEC, and one thing that is done routinely is that a nurse will aspirate the nasogastric tube to ensure that there's nothing in the stomach. And by nothing, I mean usually bile. If there's bile in the stomach then it could indicate that there is some -- that there is necrotising enterocolitis beginning to form or that there might be some kind of obstruction, you know, in the bowel.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But it's not just a matter of nasogastric aspirations, you're also keeping a careful eye on the baby, particularly its
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: abdomen. Therefore we've heard about abdomens being examined and being soft, which is normal, or distended, which means they're full of something, usually air. And also you look at the overall well-being of the baby because obviously if there is a serious abdominal condition, then that's going to impact on the whole baby and, as we've heard previously, the heart rate will increase, the oxygen requirement would increase, the baby may have irregular breathing. blocks.text: If you've got a serious abdominal problem, you're not going to do any of that. Therefore he would have been a good baby. And we also know he had an ultrasound scan of his head, which was normal, great. So therefore he was a feisty baby, he was doing very satisfactorily.

blocks.text: The next heading you gave us was one of infection.

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Now, the important thing about that is that it had increased because the normal value is less than 10, so it was up to 23, not particularly high, to be frank, you know. blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The other marker, which is a non-specific marker of infection, I suppose, is that his platelet count fell.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: There was a value of 90 recorded and a value of 40 recorded.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Values of 90 or 40 on their own don't tell you very much, but if you've got a CRP that's increased and you have an X-ray that's not normal, the low platelet count was probably a non-specific marker of his infection.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. In terms of some sort of -- no, I'll move on to, I think, the fourth heading you gave us, which was the metabolism or met --

blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: There were other markers showing that he was getting satisfactory oxygenation anyway, so therefore metabolic-wise he was a very stable little baby.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You mentioned earlier, when you were giving us the four headings that we're presently deal with, the issue of jaundice and bilirubin.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's another metabolic issue. All premature babies become jaundiced. Babies are born with a high haemoglobin. The red cells don't live so long. So as they die, they'll release -well, a substance that makes them look jaundiced, becomes jaundiced.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The good news with [Baby C] was that his jaundice values were very, very satisfactory. He did not become severely jaundiced. If you are severely jaundiced you need phototherapy. His condition was so good, they stopped his phototherapy quickly.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The other useful point about his bilirubin being not particularly high is that an infection that is not that controlled can damage your red blood cells, so an increased jaundice is another marker of infection.
