blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. So lest it's not clear from the evidence you've given us so far, Dr Evans, where was his infection?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In his lung.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And what was the infection, what label would you put on it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I would just call it pneumonia. Blood cultures were carried out, but as far as I know, no organisms were grown. This is very common in babies because, as I think we've heard from one of the doctors, because we are so concerned about infection in premature babies, one tends to do blood cultures and other blood tests, but you do not wait to get the result before starting antibiotics.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. Does it come to the fact that you assume -- as you do the test, you assume you're going to get a bad result?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So you start to -- you hope for the best but prepare for the worst so to speak?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's absolutely correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So you treat for what you fear may be the result of the test but you don't wait for the result before treating?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That is correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: All right. In your opinion, taking into account all the evidence you have read and heard, did breathing issues have any direct cause -- were they the cause for [Baby C]'s collapse?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No. The breathing issues cannot explain his collapse.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Feeding issues, and by that I'm including a blockage of the gut or NEC or anything like that, did that cause [Baby C]'s collapse?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, that cannot explain his collapse either.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The infection that you've told us he had, namely pneumonia, did that cause his collapse?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No. No, his infection was under control. Not completely resolved, but it would not cause a collapse and certainly not a collapse, as it were, out of the blue.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So if a baby with that sort of infection is on a pathway to collapse, what would one expect to see?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. We are familiar with treating pneumonia and if the treatment is not working, babies get worse. There are a number of markers that give you warning your treatment isn't working.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: First of all, you may get an increase in heart rate.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did we see that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Which did not occur. I've seen his monitoring charts and his heart rate is nice and steady, within the normal range, all the way until the collapse. So his heart rate didn't change at all in the hours prior to his death.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Respiratory rate, the same. It stayed within the norm.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Even more useful, in my experience, is oxygen saturation, sats. They remained absolutely where they should be, high 90s, throughout. So therefore, his oxygen saturations did not drop.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but in terms of his oxygen saturations, in the context of an infection to the lungs, namely pneumonia, does the oxygen saturation have a bearing on your view about the part that pneumonia might have played?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Oh, absolutely, because if the pneumonia is getting worse, then your saturations will fall and/or -- the two go together -- if the oxygen level does fall, then the clinical team would increase his oxygen requirement. So therefore, he was on 25%, hardly any additional oxygen at all, but if his pneumonia was getting worse or had been getting worse during the previous few hours, then what you'd find is the oxygen requirement would have gone up, in other words the staff would
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: have increased the oxygen requirement to keep the saturations at a satisfactory level.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: None of this was necessary, so this is why clinically, his respiratory status was very, very stable, under control.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. And finally, the metabolic issues, namely the glucose and the jaundice. Did they have any bearing on [Baby C]'s collapse?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: None at all. Several glucose values were done in the -well, throughout his life. Apart from one, the values in the last day, all within normal values. Bilirubin had flattened out, great. And again, what we call blood gas values, there were a number of them and they weren't showing any trends, you know, worrying trends. They all fluctuate a bit from one test to the other, but the capillary values -- sorry, the capillary blood gases were all again as you would expect in a baby like [Baby C].
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. And so what in your opinion, Dr Evans, was the cause of [Baby C]'s catastrophic collapse and death?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right. During my preliminary report I didn't come to any conclusion at all. I just thought that this was difficult to explain for the reasons we've gone through.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So we've had to go through possibilities.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: In passing, one of the cases we're talking about is a little baby called [Baby G]. I'm not going to mention anything about her now obviously, but one problem that can cause a baby to suddenly stop breathing is if the abdomen is filled with air or filled with oxygen, filled with gas under pressure. A baby can tolerate a certain amount of gas in its abdomen, you know, that's not a problem, because we see that with CPAP.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But if you get a significant injection of air into the stomach, it will cause what we call splinting of the diaphragm. Now, the diaphragm is a muscle that sits between the abdomen and the lungs and the diaphragm has to move up and down for people to be able to breathe properly. If you get a load of pressure in your abdomen, that diaphragm can't move and you then get the socalled splintage and you will soon suffocate, you won't be able to breathe and you can collapse pretty quickly.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So therefore, his collapse is consistent with a volume of air injected into his stomach, it splints the diaphragm, stops breathing, he's less than 800 grams, so that's what happens.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Okay. I just want to -- because this is, as you've already alluded to, at least in passing, this is or may become a recurring theme in this case. All right? So I'd just like you to give the jury a bit more of an explanation.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Is the position this, that the lungs are in the upper part of the chest?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: One on either side.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Mm.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Beneath the lungs is a muscle called the diaphragm?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You said the diaphragm moves down as you breathe in?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So is the effect of it moving down to cause negative pressure in the upper chest?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, to suck oxygen, air, into your lungs, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: All right. But the diaphragm can move down normally, but if, underneath the diaphragm, the stomach is pumped full of air, what effect does that have on the movement of the diaphragm?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It stops the diaphragm moving effectively.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And the effect of that is what?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: If the diaphragm is unable to move effectively, then your lungs cannot get air into them, cannot get fresh air or fresh oxygen. Without fresh oxygen you become hypoxic, in other words you lack oxygen, and obviously you cannot survive without oxygen, thus a collapse.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. Now, in the context of [Baby C]'s death, have you seen an expert report written by a pathologist called Dr Andreas Marnerides?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I have.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Have you also had an opportunity of discussing this case with Dr Marnerides at all or have you simply been limited to reading his report?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think I discussed it -- yes, I have discussed it with him.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: In coming to your view, have you taken into account the findings of Dr Marnerides?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I have.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I won't ask you any more about that. If anybody else wants to ask you, they can.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Can I just have a moment, please, my Lord?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: (Pause)
Those are all the questions I have at this stage, thank you.
It's a little early for a break, my Lord, but for various reasons there's something I would like to consider before I cross-examine Dr Evans --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: -- as to matters arising now.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'd be grateful. Maybe 15 minutes is all we require.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Will 15 minutes be enough?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It should be, yes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It's going to be earlier than it should be, but Mr Myers wants a break and he should have a break to consider this matter, so this will be an early afternoon break. Thank you very much. But the only one, I'm hoping.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the absence of the jury)
(The witness withdrew)
We're grateful for that, my Lord, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: (A short break)
I'm grateful for the time, my Lord, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you. Jury in, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the presence of the jury)
Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Dr Evans, you've explained today that your conclusion is that the cause of death in [Baby C]'s case arose from the splinting of his diaphragm.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That is -- the mechanics of that, yes, is correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You've had the relevant clinical material and the statements relating to [Baby C] for over 5 years or thereabouts, 4.5 years, haven't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You've considered other cases featuring in this trial where you have provided reports giving the opinion that splinting of the diaphragm is a cause of death, like [Baby G], haven't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Before today, just now, you've never suggested that splinting of the diaphragm on 13 June is the cause of death for [Baby C], have you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: This is the first time we're hearing it right now, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You are alert to the possibility of splinting of a diaphragm from the other cases you've looked at, aren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Your opinion, I'm going to suggest, and as far as you can go on the material available to you alone, would not take us to splinting of the diaphragm on 13 June, would it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, I don't jump to conclusions, so therefore, as we discussed earlier, this death was unexpected and could not be explained as a result of one or more of the usual illnesses that premature babies get. Doctors work as a team. We rely on opinion
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: from other sources. And if you look at the combination of what I thought his clinical situation was, plus what I've read from Dr Marnerides' report and others, and on top of that the gaseous distension in the stomach, putting it all together that is an acceptable cause of collapse in my opinion.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: If you really thought that splinting of the diaphragm in the case of [Baby C] was a cause of collapse, you would have said that before today, Dr Evans.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not necessarily. I think when I came to this court first of all, I said that having prepared these reports initially over 5 years ago, in virtually all of the cases I've benefited from additional information since then, you know, from other experienced medical people, and if you receive additional information from other people in other disciplines, which allows you as a clinician to change or modify your opinion, that is what doctors do.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I was functioning very much as a clinician in any case of this nature.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I suggest, Dr Evans, you have been driven by something which leads you to support the allegation rather than something based on the facts beneath it. That's what's going on here, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No. The fact is this baby collapsed having been stable up until more or less the minute of his collapse and therefore one has to explain that.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I just want to deal with what you have said in -- is it eight reports that you've prepared in the case of [Baby C] plus one joint report? That's correct, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think so, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. And again, just to make it quite clear, in not one of them before today have you suggested that splinting of the diaphragm on 13 June was a cause of death?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That is correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The first report that we heard about, which is on 7 November 2017 -- in that report, Dr Evans, you said that, your paragraph 33:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "One may never know the cause of [Baby C]'s collapse, he was at great risk of unexpected collapse."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's paragraph 33 of that first report.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: All of this is correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So you agree he, in fact, was at great risk of unexpected collapse?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: He was at risk of one or more of the complications you get in preterm babies we discussed earlier.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Your words are --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry, sorry, sorry, but although he was at risk of them, he was in a neonatal unit, designated to look after him, with continuous monitoring of essential criteria such as oxygen, et cetera. So therefore, the risk was there. This is why neonatal units exist: they are to look after babies at risk of death, collapse or serious injury. Therefore the risk was there and if he had not collapsed on the 13th, he could well have -- you know, the risks were there until he was much bigger.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So the risk is there, the risk is there constantly, but those -but although the risk was there, I was satisfied, what on earth is going on here -- I think we heard Dr Gibbs say he couldn't explain why this baby collapsed either. That's a pretty straightforward statement, actually. One may never identify the cause of [Baby C]'s collapse.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Are you saying --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm not the only doctor giving evidence on this particular baby and therefore they will give evidence in due course. So that's as far as I could get based on the information I had in 2017.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Let's be clear: what you say there, based upon the records that you had access to and those statements at that point, was one may never identify the cause of his collapse?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You were ready to acknowledge that then?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And you were ready to acknowledge he was at great risk of unexpected collapse; do you agree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, yes, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You also formed the view that you cannot exclude the role of infection in his collapse; paragraph 34.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. I think -- yes, I am quite happy to elaborate on that.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Let me just ask before you do. That's on the basis of the sort of material in the medical notes that we've been looking at now, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And faced with that, back in 2017, you were able to say that we cannot exclude the role of infection, weren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Infection was a factor in [Baby C]'s short life. We know that. We know he had pneumonia. So it was a factor.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It is possible to suggest that if he did not have pneumonia, he may not have suffered the collapse -- no, I want to rephrase that.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: His pneumonia was under control. His pneumonia was under control. That's the important thing. He was on antibiotics, he was requiring hardly any additional oxygen, and his saturations were spot on. So therefore, his pneumonia was under control.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But it's my role -- I was investigating this unexpected collapse, it was my role not to -- to give an impartial view looking at all the issues, looking at all these issues. In other words, I don't prepare partisan reports, so therefore if you've got a CRP of 22, I've got to bear it in mind. If you've got an X-ray that shows pneumonia, I have to bear it in mind. Are a CRP of 22 and a pneumonia on X-ray in a baby requiring 25% oxygen sufficient explanation to cause his collapse? In my opinion, no.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Your opinion -- sorry, Dr Evans, please continue if there's more.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I've finished.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Your opinion, do you agree, in that report was that you cannot exclude the role of infection?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Infection was a part of [Baby C]'s general status during his life.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You didn't say in that report infection was part of his general status. Dealing with your opinion as to death, you said you cannot exclude the role of infection in his collapse. It's there, Dr Evans.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Infection was a factor in his life. Did it contribute...? It didn't cause his death. That's what I believe, didn't kill him.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Saying you cannot exclude the role of infection in his collapse acknowledges that it may have played a part, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It may have -- it was a contributory factor. We've heard about the four main contributory factors earlier today.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Well, now you've come to give evidence to the jury, on the same occasion that you introduce splinting of the diaphragm, you have today discounted infection in any way, haven't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I have not discounted infection. I have explained to everybody that the report of Dr Marnerides, who's the pathologist, highlights the issue of abdominal distension causing the diaphragm -- causing splinting of the diaphragm.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Now --
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Can I just ask you something about that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Please do.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You are not just here to repeat what's in the report of Dr Marnerides, are you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I am here -- right. What we do as clinicians is this: we base our opinion on an accumulation of information.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Okay? Nothing to do with being in a court or anything.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We rely on three items of information: the history, the examination and the investigations. So we put all of that together.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: In a patient who sadly dies, we then turn to pathologists to see if they can enlighten us on information that we are not too certain about. There's no point in getting a pathology opinion — if I knew everything I would not need a pathology opinion.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So therefore, you need all of those things. The greater the bits of information you have, then the more likely you are in reaching a diagnosis. So in this particular baby, I'm not going to repeat what I said earlier, we know the history, he was a preterm baby, we know what the examination findings showed, we know what the investigations showed. The markers of infection are pretty marginal, a CRP of 22, in an otherwise -- a baby who wasn't -- just had an infection -- it's important, Mr Myers, to
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: know -- he was recovering from an infection. If I didn't say that too clearly in my report, well, there we are.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But his supportive therapy wasn't getting worse, it was getting less, because for the last 12 hours of his life he was off his CPAP, right? He was off his CPAP.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: All he had was Optiflow, which is basically nasal prongs to deliver -- so you know exactly what percentage of oxygen the baby's getting.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So therefore, respiratory-wise, he wasn't even staying the same, he was improving.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Can I ask you this, Dr Evans: are you trying to use what you anticipate will be the evidence of Dr Marnerides, the pathologist, to find a way of producing an allegation as to the harm that was done on the 13th --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, no --
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- which you haven't made before today?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry, this baby was put in harm's way.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: That's something, so far as the 13th is concerned, that until you gave your evidence now, you have not identified to this point on the 13th, have you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: What I did initially was --
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Can I ask that first, please? Can you answer that question (overspeaking).
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Ask it again.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You have not in these reports, up until your evidence now, identified any specific way in which he was put in harm's way on 13 June, have you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not in this first report, no.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And you are coming up with things here now, as we go along, to try to support an allegation of harm on 13 June, aren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I'm coming up with clinically proven mechanisms that explain why babies collapse.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Well, let's move then to your next report, the second one -- one specific reference was made to it -- of 31 May 2018, 6 months after the first one.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: In that report you say at paragraph 36, having had time to reflect from the first report:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "One may never identify the cause of [Baby C]'s collapse."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That is correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: "He was at great risk of unexpected collapse."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: That was your considered opinion, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it was.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And that's the position, isn't it, one may never identify the cause of [Baby C]'s collapse and he's at great risk of unexpected collapse?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Right. He was at great risk, okay? He was at great risk. There's quite a big difference between being at risk of unexpected collapse and actually finding a cause for it. Again, as I have said, as a clinician, you play as a team, and part of your team in a child who sadly dies is the pathology.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Is your team the other prosecution experts, Dr Evans?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, no.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Who's your team, so we can be clear?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The medical team. I have not seen any report that comes up with an explanation regarding [Baby C]'s collapse other than what I have said today and what Dr Marnerides has said in his report and what other people will say.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I have read reports that are -- I don't mean this disrespectfully -- I've read reports that come up with this idea and that idea and the other idea and all that sort of stuff, which is very interesting to me because I'm a clinician, I want to know what could have caused all this, but I have not seen a single report -- and I am happy to be corrected on this one -- I have not seen a single medical report that says I am wrong, [Baby C] died because of something else. I have not seen a
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: single report that gets off the fence and tells me that. I am happy to be corrected, Mr Myers, but I have not.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Therefore this would always be -- this case, right?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: This case would always be a challenging case for any clinician and it's a challenging case because we know of his various pathological problems, so it is quite difficult to separate the pathological problems, infection, feeding, et cetera, that we heard about earlier, it's quite difficult to separate those from an event where he was placed in harm's way as a result of some kind of deliberate act.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Now, I don't think I could do that alone. But putting all the evidence together, then that is where we are.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I'm looking at what you say here, Dr Evans. You don't mention in this report, the second one we came to, anything about splinting of the diaphragm on the 13th, do you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, no, you've said that several times and we have all heard it.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: There are several reports, aren't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: In none of which do you mention splinting of the diaphragm on the 13th, do you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, you have mentioned that and I have said, no, there isn't.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You also in this report, paragraph 37, repeat that you cannot exclude the role of infection in his collapse, don't you? Paragraph 37.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It is a factor in his general status, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And that's the truth of the matter, isn't it? You cannot exclude infection from his collapse?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: What you cannot do, you cannot exclude infection as a factor in his general status. What I can do, looking at all of this -- remember I prepared a load of reports looking at all of this -- is this. He's got an infection but it's under control. And we all -- you know, I've listened to the evidence from the other people. We've all heard the evidence from the local teams --
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It's your evidence we're looking at now, Dr Evans.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I'm aware of that and that's my evidence.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Let's move forward to about a year or so later, 26 March 2019, the next report. Paragraph 13.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't have paragraphs on my copy. Hang on.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It's page 6 of 7.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I beg your pardon, I do.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Two things here, page 6 of 7. Having reviewed all of this, about a year later, you say -- and it's in the centre of that paragraph:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "It's therefore probable that infection was a significant factor in [Baby C]'s collapse during the late hours of 13 June 2015."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, yes, I've seen that, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And you recognised then that infection may be a significant factor in his collapse, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That was my opinion at the time and, as I have said, if, as a clinician, I receive additional information that allows me to change my opinion or modify my opinion, that is what we do as clinicians.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But nothing has changed with regard to evidence of infection, Dr Evans, since then. You may have heard other things from Dr Marnerides, but nothing's changed on the evidence of infection, has it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, he had an infection, he had pneumonia, it was -- on the monitoring that was present on the little baby, his monitoring was fine.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: As well as that, he was actually taken off CPAP for a couple of times to have skin-to-skin with his parents, and so that isn't something you do if you are worried or concerned about a baby's condition, you wouldn't take them off CPAP. He managed very well.

blocks.text: So this was a baby who had known risk factors, but actually was not only doing very well but was actually improving in that he had been stepped down from CPAP to Optiflow and his -- the amount of inspired oxygen, the extra oxygen he was given, had also reduced.

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We've also heard that until about 15 minutes before his collapse, he hadn't been fed in effect for over 3 days.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Or not fed enteral feeds, I should say, for over 3 days.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Is that standard practice?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's standard practice for any baby where there has been a concern about the placental blood flow because we know that those babies are at high risk of necrotising enterocolitis, so
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: the rationale is that you just rest the gut and when babies are stable you give very small amounts of milk down the nasogastric tube in a very controlled way so that if the baby doesn't tolerate the feed for any reason, you can stop and reassess the situation. So this would be absolutely standard.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you. So far as the -- just going back to the issue that you spoke of earlier concerning the gas in [Baby C]'s stomach on the 12th, did you go to the records to see what, if any, evidence there was concerning whether or not that had been aspirated or what might have been the cause of that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did go to the records to have a look because babies who are on CPAP can accumulate gas in their tummy and in their gut. That can make the gut swell and in turn press up on the diaphragm. In order to minimise the effect of that, the nursing staff would aspirate the nasogastric tube and either they may get some stomach contents or milk, if a baby's being fed, or they may get copious amounts of air. It's usual practice to note down the volumes of air that you've aspirated to give the medical staff and other nurses an idea of how much air a baby is accumulating. I couldn't find any evidence that those volumes of air were recorded or if any gas at all was aspirated. They may have been by nursing staff, but they weren't recorded.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And the other thing that's a difficulty for me was that for babies not fed, if the nurses -- well, as well as aspirating the tube, the nursing staff certainly wherever I've worked would also put the tube on free drainage so they would leave the top of the nasogastric tube open so that air can come out on its own and either attach that to a bag or just leave it free. And also, actively aspirate every 4 hours or 2 hours, whatever is deemed appropriate.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: There was only fleeting mention of the tube being on free drainage, so I don't know (a) if the tubes were aspirated regularly and air was aspirated or if the tube was on free drainage. And if neither of those things happened, then gas would accumulate within the stomach and would have caused that X-ray appearance.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And this is gas from what source, sorry, just to be clear?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: From the CPAP.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That's the 12th. What about the 13th? Were the records any different so far as the information they imparted as to whether the NGT was being aspirated and/or whether it was on free drainage?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We know the nasogastric tube was being aspirated because there's evidence of 0.5ml of fluid that is written down.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: There is no record if any additional air was aspirated.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Within the narrative, the nurse during the day has written that actually [Baby C] had two tubes replaced, two of the tubes were orogastric as opposed to nasogastric, so they went into his mouth and down into his tummy.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Two of those were replaced during the day because he was very active and, finally, a third tube, which was a nasogastric tube, was replaced.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What I don't know is when those tubes came out and when they were replaced or what the time frame was between one tube coming out and the next tube going in because, of course, if that happened over several hours or while he was out with his parents, air would accumulate in his tummy and have no way of escape and there isn't a record of that, I'm afraid. So it's difficult to know how effective the nurses were at trying to get rid of the accumulated air.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In the narrative there is mention of the tube being on free drainage, but it's not clear whether that was for the entire shift or just after the nasogastric tube was passed, which was when [Baby C] went on to the Optiflow from the CPAP.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And that would have been after the X-ray film taken with the long line in --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: -- and the bubble in the stomach, as it was described?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Taking a step back then and helping us with the possible causes of why it was [Baby C] had this bubble in his stomach on 12 June, what conclusions did you reach?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: If the tube -- the nursing care of the nasogastric tube meant that the tube was not on free drainage and was not aspirated, then it could well have been down to accumulation of gas by CPAP. The alternative explanation is that there was a deliberate introduction of air down that tube.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. In that context does the views that were being expressed at the time, so for example by Dr Beech, who we heard from -- are they important or are they not important?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The medical staff at the time were clear that the abdomen was soft, that the baby was well, so they didn't appear to be concerned about the abdomen.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. I'm looking to paragraph 5.16 now, please. When you looked for a reason for [Baby C]'s collapse at about 11.15 or so on 13 June, could you find an explanation?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No. Babies like this don't just suddenly collapse. You get prior warning that something is amiss, they do not go from being stable to a cardiorespiratory arrest situation within minutes. So the kind of conditions that could cause problems within the gut I know [Baby C] didn't have, but in any case they would not have caused this sudden and catastrophic collapse which was unresponsive to resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Premature babies do get infections and do become unwell. They rarely collapse in this way or it'd be very unusual for them to collapse in this way, but they usually are responsive to resuscitation and he wasn't.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So in that context, in your view, did the infection which [Baby C] had -- was that the cause of his catastrophic collapse?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No. I think he died with his pneumonia, not because of his pneumonia.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you very much. Those are all the questions I have for you.
